article.overview: A plasma temperature sensor measures the temperature of charged particles (electrons and, in some designs, ions) in the thin ionised gas that surrounds a planetary body. Near the Moon, this plasma is produced when sunlight and the solar wind interact with the surface and with the very tenuous lunar exosphere. Electron temperature is one of the basic quantities that describe this environment, alongside plasma density, and it is usually obtained from the current measured by an electrically biased probe. The best-documented flown example is the Langmuir probe RAMBHA-LP on India's Chandrayaan-3 lander, which operated on the lunar surface near the south pole in August and September 2023. A second, more recent design, the Multi-Needle Langmuir Probe (m-NLP) developed by Norway and ESA partners, was prepared for a lunar surface flight on the UAE's Rashid rover, but that rover was lost when the Hakuto-R lander failed in April 2023. The m-NLP has therefore not been confirmed to have made lunar measurements. No images have been included because no direct official image asset URL was verified during this run.
article.description: The name 'plasma temperature sensor' describes the measured quantity, not a single standard instrument. In practice, a plasma temperature sensor is a sensing element placed in the ambient plasma, together with electronics that apply a controlled voltage and record the resulting current. The current-voltage relationship is then analysed to derive the electron temperature and, usually, the electron density. Two sensing styles appear in the sources reviewed. A single spherical probe on a boom, as used by RAMBHA-LP, is held away from the lander body so that the lander's own disturbance of the local plasma is reduced. A set of miniature cylindrical needles, each held at a fixed voltage, as used by the m-NLP, is described by ESA as allowing very fine spatial sampling; the m-NLP's lunar sampling rate is not given in the sources reviewed. Both approaches belong to the Langmuir probe family. A Langmuir probe is an electrode biased to a range of voltages while immersed in plasma, and the current it collects depends on the density and temperature of the charged particles and on the applied voltage.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of a lunar plasma temperature sensor is to characterise the plasma environment immediately above the surface. Electron temperature and density are needed to understand how the solar wind and the magnetospheric environment of the Earth influence the lunar near-surface plasma; how the plasma changes over the lunar day and during passages through Earth's geomagnetic tail; which ion species are present near the surface, which affects models of the lunar ionosphere; and the plasma conditions that spacecraft, instruments and astronauts experience close to the surface. The MNRAS paper on RAMBHA-LP states that the observed dayside ionosphere was modulated by solar wind and magnetospheric particle flux, and that the modulation differed inside and outside Earth's geomagnetic tail. The same paper argues that molecular species contribute to the near-surface plasma. These are interpretations reported by the authors, not settled conclusions.
article.operating_principle: A Langmuir probe is biased to a series of voltages relative to the local plasma, and the current collected at each voltage is recorded. The shape of the resulting current-voltage (I-V) curve depends on the particle densities, energies and temperatures in the plasma. From the shape of the curve, scientists can derive the electron temperature and the electron density, and the ion density and energy can be inferred from the parts of the curve dominated by ion collection. For RAMBHA-LP, the publicly reported operating parameters are a sweep bias from -12 V to +12 V and a voltage step of 0.1 V; the dwell time per step is reported inconsistently across sources (see physical_specifications). Current measurements down to picoampere levels are reported. The m-NLP uses a different strategy: its four cylinders are each held at a fixed voltage rather than swept through a range. ESA states that a conventional sweep typically lasts half a second to two seconds, whereas the m-NLP design makes much faster measurements, which permit very fine spatial sampling.
article.scientific_importance: Measurements of the plasma around the Moon help to test models of the lunar ionosphere, which is far thinner than Earth's and is strongly affected by the lunar surface and by the Earth's magnetic environment. Direct in situ measurements at the surface provide a check on remote-sensing estimates made from higher altitude. The RAMBHA-LP results illustrate this value. The MNRAS authors report that their in situ densities are 'significantly higher than estimates' from higher-altitude radio occultation observations, and the discrepancy is not resolved in the paper as summarised here. For RAMBHA-LP, the MNRAS paper reports electron temperatures of 3000 to 8000 K during the observation period, which is relevant to energy transfer in the near-surface plasma.

physical_specifications.note: There is no single universal specification for a plasma temperature sensor. The instrument class ranges from a single boom-mounted probe to a multi-element array, and mass, power and dimensions depend on the sensing configuration and electronics. Values not publicly specified are recorded as null. The examples were designed for different platforms and measurement goals and are not directly comparable.

examples.name: RAMBHA-LP (Radio Anatomy of the Moon Bound Hypersensitive ionosphere and Atmosphere - Langmuir Probe)
examples.status: Flown. Carried on the Chandrayaan-3 lander (Vikram), which landed on 23 August 2023 at the lunar south polar region; operated on the surface during the lunar day.
examples.developer: Space Physics Laboratory (SPL), Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC), Thiruvananthapuram, as reported on the ISRO instrument page.
examples.probe_geometry: Metallic spherical Langmuir probe of about 5 cm diameter (ISRO instrument summary; eoportal).
examples.mounting: Upper deck of the Chandrayaan-3 lander, on a 1 m boom that keeps the probe away from the lander body (ISRO instrument summary; eoportal).
examples.deployment: Held in a stowed configuration by a hold-and-release mechanism and deployed after lunar touchdown (ISRO instrument summary).
examples.dwell_time_per_step_ms: Unresolved. The ISRO instrument summary gives 1 millisecond. A value of 60 milliseconds was reported in a search-result summary of the SPL page for RAMBHA-LP; that SPL page could not be fetched during this run, so the 60 ms value is unverified and conflicts with the ISRO figure.
examples.current_sensitivity: Return currents as low as picoamperes (ISRO instrument summary).
examples.measured_quantities: Ion and electron densities and their energies (ISRO instrument summary); electron density and electron temperature (MNRAS paper).

reported_results.electron_density_mnras: Mean daytime electron density of 380 to 600 per cubic centimetre (MNRAS abstract).
reported_results.electron_density_isro_instrument_summary: Roughly 5 to 30 million electrons per cubic metre, equivalent to about 5 to 30 per cubic centimetre (ISRO instrument summary; eoportal).
reported_results.electron_density_discrepancy: The two density values differ by more than an order of magnitude and are not reconciled in the sources reviewed. The peer-reviewed MNRAS value is treated as the more authoritative, but the discrepancy should be checked against the paper's full text.
reported_results.observation_period: 24 August to 2 September 2023, during the lunar day (MNRAS abstract). An ISRO results article gives 23 August to 3 September 2023.
reported_results.site: South polar region; ISRO results article gives the landing site as Shiv Shakti point (69.3 degrees S, 32.3 degrees E).

examples.mass_power_dimensions_status: Not publicly specified at instrument level in the sources reviewed. Lander-level and rover-level values are whole-vehicle values and are not RAMBHA-LP values.

examples.name: Multi-Needle Langmuir Probe (m-NLP)
examples.type: Ground-tested instrument; ISS version planned; lunar version planned for the Rashid rover (not confirmed flown)
examples.status: Passed the ESA Acceptance Review after thermal vacuum testing at ESTEC (ESA article). A version for the International Space Station was planned. A smaller version was planned for the UAE's Rashid rover, which was to fly on the Hakuto-R lander; the Hakuto-R landing attempt failed on 25 April 2023, and no lunar m-NLP measurements are reported in the sources reviewed.
examples.developer: University of Oslo and Eidsvoll Electronics (Norway), with ESA co-funding through the PRODEX and GSTP programmes. Eidsvoll Electronics designed and built the electronics; the boom system was adapted from the NorSat-1 design.
examples.sensor_configuration: Four miniature cylinders, each held at a different but fixed voltage (ESA article).
examples.spatial_resolution: Less than two metres (ESA article; ISS version).
examples.measurement_rate: Almost 10000 measurements per second for the ISS version (ESA article). The lunar version's sampling rate is not stated in the sources reviewed.
examples.lunar_purpose: To survey the plasma environment immediately above the lunar surface, where regolith interacts with sunlight (ESA plasma sampler article).
examples.lunar_design_differences: Not stated beyond the difference in target environment (lunar surface versus the Station's exterior).
examples.flight_status: Lunar version not confirmed flown. ISS version launch date and flight results not stated.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No dimensions are verified for the m-NLP. RAMBHA-LP's probe diameter (about 5 cm) and boom length (1 m) are the only verified geometry values; its enclosure or electronics dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The RAMBHA-LP and m-NLP designs differ in sensing configuration: a single boom-mounted sphere versus a four-element array.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: RAMBHA-LP instrument mass is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The m-NLP mass is not stated. Whole-vehicle values for the Chandrayaan-3 lander (about 1749.86 kg including the rover) and rover (26 kg) are not instrument masses and must not be used as RAMBHA-LP values.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: RAMBHA-LP instrument power is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The m-NLP power is not stated. The lander's 738 W figure (winter solstice, eoportal) is a whole-vehicle value.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A plasma temperature sensor on the lunar surface must operate in an environment very different from near-Earth plasma. The Moon has no substantial atmosphere, the surface experiences large temperature variations between lunar day and night, and the plasma conditions change with the Moon's position relative to the solar wind and the Earth's geomagnetic tail. The RAMBHA-LP paper describes the plasma as dynamic and modulated by solar wind or geomagnetic-tail particles, depending on the Moon's position, so measurements need to be made over time to capture these changes. The probe must be exposed to the ambient plasma and kept clear of the lander's own plasma disturbance; for RAMBHA-LP, the 1 m boom served this purpose. Thermal and mechanical requirements for the instrument's electronics are not documented in the sources reviewed.
article.limitations: Electron temperature and density are derived from a model fit to the probe's current-voltage curve, so results depend on the assumptions used in that fit. The RAMBHA-LP data cover about ten days at one landing site and may not represent other regions or times. The two RAMBHA-LP density values reported by ISRO and by the MNRAS paper differ by more than an order of magnitude, and the dwell time is reported differently across sources. Mass, power and dimensions are not verified for RAMBHA-LP or the m-NLP. No lunar m-NLP data are reported.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: RAMBHA-LP was a surface instrument on the Chandrayaan-3 lander. The m-NLP lunar version was planned for the Rashid rover, which was to be carried by the Hakuto-R lander; that landing attempt failed. No lunar m-NLP flight is confirmed.
transportation_process: RAMBHA-LP was carried on the upper deck of the Chandrayaan-3 lander; the sources reviewed do not describe the launch vehicle or the integration process for this instrument.
The Chandrayaan-3 lander landed on 23 August 2023, and the rover was deployed on 24 August 2023 (eoportal).
RAMBHA-LP was held stowed by a hold-and-release mechanism and deployed after touchdown (ISRO instrument summary).
The lander and rover were designed for one lunar day (14 Earth days). The lander entered sleep mode on 4 September 2023, and contact attempts on 22 September 2023 were unsuccessful (eoportal).

The m-NLP lunar version was to fly on the Rashid rover aboard Hakuto-R. The Hakuto-R landing attempt failed on 25 April 2023, and the rover was not reported to have operated on the surface (Physics World).
The m-NLP's compatibility with any lander has not been verified from primary interface documentation.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: RAMBHA-LP: hold-and-release mechanism with a 1 m boom, deployed after touchdown (ISRO instrument summary). m-NLP: not described for the lunar version in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Chandrayaan-3 (RAMBHA-LP, 2023) is the flown example. Hakuto-R Mission 1 (2023) carried the Rashid rover with the planned m-NLP lunar version; the landing attempt failed.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: RAMBHA-LP's compatibility with the Chandrayaan-3 lander is verified by flight. The m-NLP's compatibility with the Hakuto-R lander or any other lander is not verified. Lander-level mass, power and dimensions (eoportal: 1749.86 kg including the rover, 738 W at winter solstice, 2000 x 2000 x 1166 mm) are whole-vehicle values and are not instrument interface specifications.

article.historical_significance: RAMBHA-LP provided in situ measurements of the lunar near-surface plasma at the south polar region during the Chandrayaan-3 mission, and the MNRAS paper is a peer-reviewed analysis of those measurements that compares them with higher-altitude estimates. The m-NLP is significant as a design example: it represents a new approach to Langmuir probe measurement that was prepared for lunar use, but its planned lunar mission was not completed.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: RAMBHA-LP density discrepancy: the ISRO instrument summary reports roughly 5 to 30 million electrons per cubic metre (about 5 to 30 per cubic centimetre), while the MNRAS paper reports 380 to 600 per cubic centimetre. The discrepancy is not explained in the sources reviewed. RAMBHA-LP dwell time: 1 millisecond per ISRO; 60 milliseconds per an SPL search-result summary that could not be verified by fetching the SPL page. Instrument mass, power and size are not publicly specified for RAMBHA-LP and not stated for the m-NLP. No lunar m-NLP measurements are reported, and the ISS version's launch date and flight results are not stated. A search summary of an ESA study suggested that Langmuir probes alone may not distinguish energetic particle populations near the lunar surface and that a retarding-potential instrument may be needed; this was not verified against the study document and is recorded only as a design consideration. Direct official image asset URLs were not verified, so no images are embedded. The MNRAS abstract was reviewed; the full text, including its uncertainty analysis, was not.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values are absent because no images are included. All source URLs in this file have query strings and fragments removed. The DOI URL is the canonical resolver link for the MNRAS paper.

data_quality_notes: RAMBHA-LP electron density is reported as 380-600 per cubic centimetre by the MNRAS paper (abstract) and as roughly 5-30 million per cubic metre (about 5-30 per cubic centimetre) by an ISRO instrument summary. The discrepancy is unresolved in the sources reviewed.

RAMBHA-LP dwell time is 1 millisecond per the ISRO instrument summary; a search-result summary of the SPL page reports 60 milliseconds. The SPL page could not be fetched (DNS failure), so the 60 ms value is unverified.
RAMBHA-LP observation period differs slightly between sources: 24 August to 2 September 2023 (MNRAS abstract) versus 23 August to 3 September 2023 (ISRO results article).

RAMBHA-LP instrument mass, power and dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed; null values are intentional. Lander-level values (1749.86 kg, 738 W, 2000 x 2000 x 1166 mm) and rover values (26 kg, 50 W) are whole-vehicle values and are not RAMBHA-LP values. Sources differ on the lander mass (1749.86 kg vs 1752 kg including the rover) and on solstice power conditions.

The m-NLP lunar version did not fly in the sources reviewed; the Hakuto-R landing attempt failed on 25 April 2023 and the Rashid rover is not reported to have operated on the surface. The m-NLP mass, size, power and lunar sampling rate are not stated.
The ESA plasma sampler article (dated 7 December 2022) describes the Hakuto-R launch as upcoming, so its mission status statements are historical and were checked against the Physics World article.

A search-result summary of an ESA study suggested a retarding-potential analyser may be needed to distinguish energetic populations near the lunar surface. This was not verified against the study document and is recorded only as a design consideration.
No direct official image asset URLs were verified during this run. image_urls_added is set to false and no image objects are included.
